title: Acute Appendicitis - Young Woman with Abdominal Pain
patient_instructions: You are Jenna Marsh, a 24-year-old woman in the emergency department with abdominal pain. Opening line: 'Doctor, I've been having this pain in the right lower side of my stomach. It started yesterday, it's getting worse, and I'm starting to get a bit worried.' Key story if asked: the pain STARTED around your belly button yesterday and has now SHIFTED down to the right lower side today (this migration is important - volunteer it only if asked where it began). It is a dull, vague, constant ache, about 6/10, worse today, nothing makes it better, not related to food, no radiation. You feel nauseated and may have vomited once. You have LOST YOUR APPETITE. No diarrhoea, no constipation, no fever that you know of, no blood in stool, no weight loss. No burning or frequency passing urine, no blood in urine. Your last period was 3 weeks ago and periods are regular; you are sexually active with your partner and use condoms; no vaginal bleeding or discharge. No previous surgery, no medications, no allergies. If offered a painkiller, say yes please. Your IDEAS: you think it might be something you ate. Your CONCERNS: it is getting worse and you are scared. Your EXPECTATIONS: you want the pain sorted and to know what is wrong. Affect: visibly uncomfortable, holding the right lower abdomen.
candidate_instructions: Setting: Emergency department. Jenna Marsh, a 24-year-old woman, presents with abdominal pain. Tasks: (1) Confirm haemodynamic stability, then take a focused history over approximately 4 minutes. (2) Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the patient. Consider GI, urinary (KUB) and pelvic causes. Offer analgesia appropriately. The examiner is looking for a structured pain assessment (SIQORAA), elicitation of the classic migratory pain and appetite loss, screening of the three differential groups, and a clear patient explanation.
examiner_instructions: Vitals if asked: BP 110/70, HR 88, RR 12, temp 36.5. The candidate should elicit periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant over ~24 hours, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, and exclude urinary and pelvic causes (LMP 3 weeks ago, no discharge). Reward offering timely analgesia (real Australian practice: analgesia in the acute abdomen is standard of care and does NOT mask diagnosis; allergies must be checked before charting a drug). Expected diagnosis: acute appendicitis, with differentials ectopic pregnancy, PID, ovarian cyst/torsion, UTI/cystitis, mesenteric adenitis, inguinal hernia. Expected safety points: beta-hCG in ALL women of reproductive age regardless of LMP, keep NBM, IV access/fluids, surgical referral. If migration and anorexia are not asked about, this is a significant omission. Use the rubric.

criteria: Confirms haemodynamic stability and offers analgesia appropriately
Structured pain assessment (site, migration, intensity, quality, onset, radiation, aggravating/relieving)
Screens KUB and pelvic/obstetric groups including LMP and sexual history
Identifies acute appendicitis with reasons (migratory pain, anorexia, nausea)
Gives focused differentials with brief reasons (ectopic pregnancy, PID, ovarian torsion/cyst, UTI)
Beta-hCG in all reproductive-age women, NBM, IV fluids, surgical referral
Investigations (FBE, CRP, ultrasound first-line then CT if equivocal) and red-flag escalation for perforation
Explains diagnosis simply and gives short differential with reasons; explores ICE
Empathy, analgesia, checks understanding and safety-nets

red_flags: Fever >38, generalised peritonism (rigidity/guarding), tachycardia or hypotension - suggests perforation, escalate immediately
Missed ectopic pregnancy - beta-hCG required in all women of reproductive age with abdominal pain regardless of LMP
Ovarian torsion - sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain requiring urgent gynaecology assessment
Rapidly worsening pain with signs of sepsis - urgent surgical review
australian_guidelines: eTG (Analgesia) and NSW Health pain management standards: timely analgesia in the acute abdomen is standard of care and does not mask diagnosis; check allergies and prior doses before charting

Australian ED practice: beta-hCG in ALL women of reproductive age with abdominal pain; ultrasound first-line in young women (assesses ovaries/tubes), CT if equivocal; a non-visualised appendix on ultrasound does not exclude appendicitis
Medical Board of Australia Good Medical Practice: verbal consent and a chaperone offered and documented before pelvic examination
learning_objectives: Apply the SIQORAA structure and three-group differential to acute abdominal pain
Recognise the migratory pain and anorexia of appendicitis
Exclude pregnancy and pelvic pathology in a young woman with RLQ pain
Outline safe ED management and appropriate imaging
key_points: Migration of pain from the umbilicus to the RLQ over ~24 hours is the key discriminating feature
A candidate who elicits a positive sign but never asks about anorexia, nausea and migration will not pass
Beta-hCG is mandatory in all reproductive-age women regardless of a recent normal period
Ultrasound is first-line imaging in young women to avoid radiation and assess pelvic organs
